html:
A policy in mainland China, from 1980 to 2015, that limited many families to a single child to slow population growth. Rules began in 1979 and were made national in 1980.

China's leaders feared that its population, which had nearly doubled under Mao, would swamp the gains of reform and opening. Birth rates were already falling under the earlier "later, longer, fewer" campaign of the 1970s.

How it worked:

  • Urban couples were mostly limited to one child. Rural families could often have a second if the first was a girl. Ethnic minorities had looser rules.
  • Officials enforced quotas with fines, loss of jobs and, in many places, forced sterilisations and abortions.
  • Families who complied got benefits and certificates.

Its effects are debated, since birth rates were falling anyway as China grew richer. But some results are clear:

  • A strong preference for sons led to sex-selective abortion and a skewed sex ratio, with millions more young men than women.
  • A generation of only children, the "little emperors", grew up with all the hopes of two parents and four grandparents.
  • China is ageing fast, with fewer workers to support each retiree.

The policy was eased in 2015, when all couples were allowed two children, and in 2021 three. Births kept falling anyway, and China's population began to shrink in 2022, as in Japan before it. The policy is one of the largest experiments in social engineering ever made, and a link in the long story of China's numbers that runs back to the population surge of the Qing.
sum: A policy in mainland China, from 1980 to 2015, that limited many families to a single child to slow population growth. Rules began in 1979 and were made national in 1980.
